title: Chapter 89 — Service, Retention & The Long Relationship
intro: The service partnership, retention saves, and the decade view.

sections.title: Service Is Revenue
sections.content:
The sale does not end at delivery. The post-sale relationship is where the real revenue lives — not in the first purchase, but in the second, third, fourth, and every referral that comes from each of them.

The CRM pipeline does not end at 'Delivered.' It continues through warranty follow-up, annual check-in, replacement cycle, and referral cultivation. Each stage is a revenue opportunity disguised as a service touchpoint.

Registered, followed-up customers return for the second appliance at a rate 3-4 times higher than customers who never hear from you after delivery. Laundry buyers become kitchen buyers. Single appliance buyers become package buyers. The customer who trusts you does not shop around for the next purchase — they call you.

sections.title: The Proactive Service Cadence
sections.content:
Do not wait for complaints. Call proactively on a structured cadence.

48 hours post-delivery — 'Is everything running smoothly?' 30 days post-delivery — 'How are you liking the new [appliance]? Any features you have questions about?' At the water filter replacement interval — every 6 months for most fridges. 'Time for your water filter. Want me to order one for you?' This is recurring revenue and a touchpoint.

At the one-year anniversary — 'Happy anniversary with your [appliance]! Everything still great? By the way, if anyone you know is shopping for appliances, I would love to help them.'

Each call is three things at once: a retention touchpoint, a referral opportunity, and a chance to identify the next purchase. The customer whose dishwasher you check on at 12 months might mention their laundry is getting old. That is your next sale — and it came from a 90-second phone call.

sections.title: The Service Recovery Paradox
sections.content:
A customer who had a problem resolved exceptionally is MORE loyal than one who never had a problem. This is the Service Recovery Paradox — it is proven research across multiple industries, not wishful thinking.

When something goes wrong: let them vent without interrupting. Acknowledge their emotion with their own words. Take ownership regardless of fault. Solve it with a specific timeline and your name attached to the resolution. Follow up before the deadline, even if you have no update — the call itself is the point.

After resolution, offer something tangible — an accessory, a water filter, a delivery credit. Not because you owe them — because you want to convert their complaint into a story they tell in your favour.

The angry customer who becomes a fan is your most powerful marketing asset. They tell everyone: 'I had a problem, but [your name] handled it so well I would buy from them again in a heartbeat.' That story is worth more than any ad you will ever run.
